## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.86939.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.86939.3.sa1)

Numerous neurodegenerative diseases are thought to be driven by the aggregation of proteins into insoluble filaments known as "amyloids". Despite decades of research, the mechanism by which proteins convert from the soluble to insoluble state is poorly understood. In particular, the initial nucleation step is has proven especially elusive to both experiments and simulation. This is because the critical nucleus is thermodynamically unstable, and therefore, occurs too infrequently to directly observe. Furthermore, after nucleation much faster processes like growth and secondary nucleation dominate the kinetics, which makes it difficult to isolate the effects of the initial nucleation event. In this work Kandola et al. attempt to surmount these obstacles using individual yeast cells as microscopic reaction vessels. The large number of cells, and their small size, provides the statistics to separate the cells into pre- and post-nucleation populations, allowing them to obtain nucleation rates under physiological conditions. By systematically introducing mutations into the amyloid-forming polyglutamine core of huntingtin protein, they deduce the probable structure of the amyloid nucleus. This work shows that, despite the complexity of the cellular environment, the seemingly random effects of mutations can be understood with a relatively simple physical model. Furthermore, their model shows how amyloid nucleation and growth differ in significant ways, which provides testable hypotheses for probing how different steps in the aggregation pathway may lead to neurotoxicity.

In this study Kandola et al. probe the nucleation barrier by observing a bimodal distribution of cells that contain aggregates; the cells containing aggregates have had a stochastic fluctuation allowing the proteins to surmount the barrier, while those without aggregates have yet to have a fluctuation of suitable size. The authors confirm this interpretation with the selective manipulation of the PIN gene, which provides an amyloid template that allows the system to skip the nucleation event.

In simple systems lacking internal degrees of freedom (i.e., colloids or rigid molecules) the nucleation barrier comes from a significant entropic cost that comes from bringing molecules together. In large aggregates this entropic cost is balanced by attractive interactions between the particles, but small clusters are unable to form the extensive network of stabilizing contacts present in the larger aggregates. Therefore, the initial steps in nucleation incur an entropic cost without compensating attractive interactions (this imbalance can be described as a surface tension). When internal degrees of freedom are present, such as the conformational states of a polypeptide chain, there is an additional contribution to the barrier coming from the loss of conformational entropy required to the adopt aggregation-prone state(s). In such systems the clustering and conformational processes do not necessarily coincide, and a major challenge studying nucleation is to separate out these two contributions to the free energy barrier. Surprisingly, Kandola et al. find that the critical nucleus occurs within a single molecule. This means that the largest contribution to the barrier comes from the conformational entropy cost of adopting the beta-sheet state. Once this state is attained, additional molecules can be recruited with a much lower free energy barrier.

There are several considerations in interpreting this result. First, the height of the nucleation barrier(s) comes from the relative strength of the entropic costs compared to the binding affinities. This balance determines how large a nascent nucleus must grow before it can form interactions comparable to a mature aggregate. In amyloid nuclei the first three beta strands form immature contacts consisting of either side chain or backbone contacts, whereas the fourth strand is the first that is able to form both kinds of contacts (as in a mature fibril). This study used relatively long polypeptides of 60 amino acids. This is greater than the 20-40 amino acids found in amyloid-forming molecules like ABeta or IAPP. As a result, Kandola et al.'s molecules are able to fold enough times to create four beta strands and generate mature contacts intramolecularly. This authors make the plausible claim that these intramolecular folds explain the well-known length threshold (L~35) observed in polyQ diseases. The intramolecular folds reduce the importance of clustering multiple molecules together and increase the importance of the conformational states. Similarly, manipulating the sequence or molecular concentrations will be expected to manipulate the relative magnitude of the binding affinities and the clustering entropy, which will shift the relative heights of the entropic barriers.

The authors make an important point that the structure of the nucleus does not necessarily resemble that of the mature fibril. They find that the critical nucleus has a serpentine structure that is required by the need to form four beta strands to get the first mature contacts. However, this structure comes at a cost because residues in the hairpins cannot form strong backbone or zipper interactions. Mature fibrils offer a beta sheet template that allows incoming molecules to form mature contacts immediately. Thus, it is expected that the role of the serpentine nucleus is to template a more extended beta sheet structure that is found in mature fibrils.

A second point of consideration is the striking homogeneity of the nucleus structure they describe. This homogeneity is likely to be somewhat illusory. Homopolymers, like polyglutamine, have a discrete translational symmetry, which implies that the hairpins needed to form multiple beta sheets can occur at many places along the sequence. The asparagine residues introduced by the authors place limitations on where the hairpins can occur, and should be expected to increase structural homogeneity. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate that polyglutamine chains close to the minimum length of ~35 will have strict limitations on where the folds must occur in order to attain the required four beta strands.

A novel result of this work is the observation of multiple concentration regimes in the nucleation rate. Specifically, they report a plateau-like regime at intermediate regimes in which the nucleation rate is insensitive to protein concentration. The authors attribute this effect to the "self-poisoning" phenomenon observed in growth of some crystals. This is a valid comparison because the homogeneity observed in NMR and crystallography structures of mature fibrils resemble a one-dimensional crystal. Furthermore, the typical elongation rate of amyloid fibrils (on the order of one molecule per second) is many orders of magnitude slower than the molecular collision rate (by factors of 10^6 or more), implying that the search for the beta-sheet state is very slow. This slow conformational search implies the presence of deep kinetic traps that would be prone to poisoning phenomena. However, the observation of poisoning in nucleation during nucleation is striking, particularly in consideration of the expected disorder and concentration sensitivity of the nucleus. Kandola et al.'s structural model of an ordered, intramolecular nucleus explains why the internal states responsible for poisoning are relevant in nucleation.

To achieve these results the authors used a novel approach involving a systematic series of simple sequences. This is significant because, while individual experiments showed seemingly random behavior, the randomness resolved into clear trends with the systematic approach. These trends provided clues to build a model and guide further experiments.

There has been discussion in the review process about whether a monomeric nucleus is consistent with established properties of huntingtin aggregation. I do not see a problem with an energetically unfavorable conformational state preceding a concentration-dependent growth step. The authors make the case for this sequence using a schematic free energy landscape (Fig 6) that has many similarities to a free energy landscape derived from models of polyQ nucleation (Phan et al. 2022, see Fig. 6). The theory does not consider molecules large enough to form the conformational state described by Kandola et al., but the transition state is otherwise very similar.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.86939.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.86939.3.sa2)

Kandola et al. explore the important and difficult question regarding the initiating event that triggers (nucleates) amyloid fibril growth in glutamine-rich domains. The researchers use a fluorescence technique that they developed, dAMFRET, in a yeast system where they can manipulate the expression level over several orders of magnitude, and they can control the length of the polyglutamine domain as well as the insertion of interfering non-glutamine residues. Using flow cytometry, they can interrogate each of these yeast 'reactors' to test for self-assembly.

In the introduction, the authors provide a fairly thorough yet succinct review of the relevant literature into the mechanisms of polyglutamine-mediated aggregation over the last two decades, as well as a fairly clear description of the experimental techniques they developed.

Their assay shows that the fraction of cells with AmFRET signal increases strongly with an increase in polyQ length, with a threshold around 35-40 glutamines. This roughly correlates with the Q-length dependence of disease. The experiments in which asparagine or other amino acids are inserted at variable positions in the glutamine repeat are creative and thorough, and the data along with the simulations provide compelling support for the proposed Q zipper model. The experiments are strongly supportive of a model where formation of the beta-sheet nucleus is within a monomer. This is a potentially important result, as there are conflicting data in the literature as to whether the nucleus in polyQ is monomer.

The authors present convincing data that there are differences in the structural stability of their "QU" versus "QB" aggregates. However, the conclusion that "QB" must have multilamellar architecture versus "QU" was feasible but less compelling.

The authors present intriguing data showing that amyloid formation does not monotonically increase with increasing concentration, and their conclusion that high concentrations of polyQ can 'self-poison' amyloid growth is supported by the experimental data. The discussion surrounding the mechanism by which 'self-poisoning' occurs is confusing. The authors variously discuss that soluble oligomers must be the inhibitory species, that dead-end products of Q zipper nuclei are the inhibitory species, or that self-poisoning occurs because conformational conversion at the templating surface is slow relative to the rate of arrival of new molecules to the surface. The data seem consistent with an argument that, at high concentrations, non-structured polyQ oligomers form which interfere with elongation into structured amyloid assemblies - but it is not clear why such oligomers would be zippers.

Overall, this is a very valuable and thorough exploration of the fundamental question as to the nature and identity of the nucleating species in polyglutamine aggregation.

claims.source: In humans, it is responsible for nine invariably fatal neurodegenerative diseases, the most prevalent of which is Huntington's Disease.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about polyQ diseases in the field.

claims.claim: Cells exhibiting polyQ pathology die independently and stochastically with a constant frequency.
claims.source: Cells exhibiting polyQ pathology, whether in Huntington's disease patients, tissue culture, organotypic brain slices, or animal models, die independently and stochastically with a constant frequency (Clarke et al., 2000; Linsley et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Clarke et al., 2000 and Linsley et al., 2019.

claims.claim: PolyQ aggregation occurs stochastically in cells.
claims.source: First, polyQ aggregation itself occurs stochastically in cells (Colby et al., 2006; Kakkar et al., 2016; Sinnige et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Colby et al., 2006; Kakkar et al., 2016; Sinnige et al., 2021.

claims.claim: PolyQ disease onset and progression are determined almost entirely by a genetically encoded expansion in the number of sequential glutamines beyond a protein-specific threshold of approximately 36 residues.
claims.source: Second, polyQ disease onset and progression are determined almost entirely by an intramolecular change, specifically, a genetically encoded expansion in the number of sequential glutamines beyond a protein-specific threshold of approximately 36 residues (Lieberman et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lieberman et al., 2019.

claims.claim: PolyQ disease severity generally does not worsen with gene dosage.
claims.source: Unlike other amyloid diseases (Book et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2020; Selkoe and Hardy, 2016), polyQ disease severity generally does not worsen with gene dosage (Cubo et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2019; Wexler et al., 1987)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cubo et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2019; Wexler et al., 1987.

claims.claim: The rate-determining step in neuronal death occurs in a fixed minor fraction of the polyglutamine molecules.
claims.source: polyQ disease severity generally does not worsen with gene dosage (Cubo et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2019; Wexler et al., 1987), implying that the rate-determining step in neuronal death occurs in a fixed minor fraction of the polyglutamine molecules.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that disease severity does not worsen with gene dosage.

claims.claim: Amyloid nuclei cannot be observed directly by any existing experimental approach.
claims.source: Amyloid nuclei cannot be observed directly by any existing experimental approach.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current experimental methods, based on established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Amyloid nuclei are unstable by definition.
claims.source: This is because unlike mature amyloid fibrils, which are stable and amenable to structural biology, nuclei are unstable by definition.
claims.evidence: This is a definitional statement about the nature of nuclei based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: The structures of amyloid nuclei do not necessarily propagate into or correspond with the structures of mature amyloids that arise from them.
claims.source: Their structures do not necessarily propagate into or correspond with the structures of mature amyloids that arise from them (Auer et al., 2008; Buell, 2017; Erdemir et al., 2009; Hsieh et al., 2017; Levin et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2018; Li et al., 2010; Phan and Schmit, 2020; Sil et al., 2018; Yamaguchi et al., 2005; Zanjani et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Amyloid nucleation by a full length polypeptide occurs far too infrequently, and involves far too many degrees of freedom, to simulate with high resolution from a naive state.
claims.source: Moreover, amyloid nucleation by a full length polypeptide occurs far too infrequently, and involves far too many degrees of freedom, to simulate with high resolution from a naive state (Barrera et al., 2021; Kar et al., 2011; Strodel, 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barrera et al., 2021; Kar et al., 2011; Strodel, 2021.

claims.claim: Amyloid formation involves a major loss of intramolecular entropy.
claims.source: Unlike phase separation, which primarily concerns a loss of intermolecular entropy, amyloid formation additionally involves a major loss of intramolecular entropy.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the thermodynamic nature of amyloid formation based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: Nucleation selects for a specific combination of backbone and side chain torsion angles.
claims.source: That is, nucleation selects for a specific combination of backbone and side chain torsion angles (Khan et al., 2018; Vitalis and Pappu, 2011; Zhang and Schmit, 2016c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Khan et al., 2018; Vitalis and Pappu, 2011; Zhang and Schmit, 2016c.

claims.claim: Amyloid-forming proteins can accumulate to supersaturating concentrations while remaining soluble.
claims.source: As a consequence, amyloid-forming proteins can accumulate to supersaturating concentrations while remaining soluble, thereby storing potential energy that will subsequently drive their aggregation following a stochastic nucleating event (Buell, 2017; Khan et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Buell, 2017 and Khan et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Amyloid nucleation tends to occur heterogeneously.
claims.source: Due to the improbability that the requisite increases in both density and conformational ordering will occur spontaneously at the same time (i.e. homogeneously), amyloid nucleation tends to occur heterogeneously.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the improbability of simultaneous density and conformational changes, supported by established knowledge.

claims.claim: Amyloids tend to emerge via a progression of relatively less ordered but more probable, metastable intermediates of varying stoichiometry and conformation.
claims.source: In other words, amyloids tend to emerge via a progression of relatively less ordered but more probable, metastable intermediates of varying stoichiometry and conformation (Auer et al., 2008; Buell, 2017; Hsieh et al., 2017; Levin et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2018; Li et al., 2010; Serio et al., 2000; Sil et al., 2018; Vekilov, 2012; Vitalis and Pappu, 2011; Yamaguchi et al., 2005; Zanjani et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: A major body of current opinion holds that heterogeneities tend to involve liquid-liquid phase separation.
claims.source: A major body of current opinion holds that such heterogeneities tend to involve liquid-liquid phase separation, whereby the protein first forms disordered multimers that then facilitate productive conformational fluctuations (Borcherds et al., 2021; Camino et al., 2021; Crick et al., 2013; Crick et al., 2006; Dignon et al., 2020; Fisher et al., 2021; Halfmann et al., 2011; Peskett et al., 2018; Posey et al., 2018; Vitalis and Pappu, 2011; Yang and Yang, 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations representing current scientific opinion.

claims.claim: The nature of the actual nucleus for a given amyloid can depend on the protein's sequence, concentration, and cellular factors that influence its conformation.
claims.source: Therefore, the occurrence of heterogeneities implies that the nature of the actual nucleus for a given amyloid can depend not only on the protein's sequence but also its concentration and cellular factors that influence its conformation (Bradley et al., 2002; Buell, 2017; Collinge and Clarke, 2007; Phan and Schmit, 2022; Sanders et al., 2014; Törnquist et al., 2018), as illustrated in Figure 1A.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Cells expressing Q60 partition into distinct populations that either lack or contain amyloid.
claims.source: Cells expressing Q60 partition into distinct populations that either lack (no AmFRET) or contain (high AmFRET) amyloid.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the DAmFRET experiments described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The bimodal distribution of Q60 persists even among cells with the same concentration of protein, indicating that amyloid formation is rate-limited by nucleation.
claims.source: The bimodal distribution persists even among cells with the same concentration of protein, indicating that amyloid formation is rate-limited by nucleation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of bimodal distribution at similar concentrations.

claims.claim: The nucleation barrier for N60 is so large that spontaneous amyloid formation occurs at undetectable frequencies.
claims.source: The nucleation barrier for N60 is so large that spontaneous amyloid formation occurs at undetectable frequencies.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the DAmFRET data showing no detectable amyloid formation for N60.

claims.claim: Nucleation of pathologically expanded polyQ involves segments of three glutamine (Q) residues at every other position.
claims.source: We found that nucleation of pathologically expanded polyQ involves segments of three glutamine (Q) residues at every other position.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the systematic Q/N sequence space experiments described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The pattern of Q residues at every other position encodes a four-stranded steric zipper with interdigitated Q side chains.
claims.source: We demonstrate using molecular simulations that this pattern encodes a four-stranded steric zipper with interdigitated Q side chains.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through molecular dynamics simulations described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Once formed, the Q zipper poisoned its own growth by engaging naive polypeptides on orthogonal faces.
claims.source: Once formed, the zipper poisoned its own growth by engaging naive polypeptides on orthogonal faces, in a fashion characteristic of polymer crystals with intramolecular nuclei.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data showing concentration-dependent effects on amyloid formation.

claims.claim: Self-poisoning can be exploited to block amyloid formation by genetically oligomerizing polyQ prior to nucleation.
claims.source: We further show that self-poisoning can be exploited to block amyloid formation, by genetically oligomerizing polyQ prior to nucleation.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with oligomeric fusion proteins described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Q lengths 35 and shorter lacked AmFRET, indicating a failure to aggregate or even appreciably oligomerize.
claims.source: Our data recapitulated the pathologic threshold—Q lengths 35 and shorter lacked AmFRET, indicating a failure to aggregate or even appreciably oligomerize, while Q lengths 40 and longer did acquire AmFRET in a length and concentration-dependent manner (Figure 1C–D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from DAmFRET experiments shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Q lengths 40 and longer acquired AmFRET in a length and concentration-dependent manner.
claims.source: Our data recapitulated the pathologic threshold—Q lengths 35 and shorter lacked AmFRET, indicating a failure to aggregate or even appreciably oligomerize, while Q lengths 40 and longer did acquire AmFRET in a length and concentration-dependent manner (Figure 1C–D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from DAmFRET experiments shown in the figures.

claims.claim: PolyN populates the high FRET state at much lower frequencies than polyQ even at the highest concentrations.
claims.source: We found that polyN did populate the high FRET state, but at much lower frequencies than polyQ even at the highest concentrations (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), approximately 200 µM (Khan et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from DAmFRET experiments comparing polyQ and polyN.

claims.claim: Amyloid formation for values of q<6 was limited to odd numbers 1, 3, and 5.
claims.source: Second, amyloid formation for values of q<6 was limited to odd numbers 1, 3, and 5 (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the systematic Q/N sequence experiments.

claims.claim: The relationship of amyloid formation to the number of consecutive Qs exhibited an 'odd-even effect' that saturated at six.
claims.source: That is, the relationship of amyloid formation to the number of consecutive Qs exhibited an 'odd-even effect' that saturated at six.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the pattern observed in the Q/N sequence experiments.

claims.claim: The odd-even effect results from the Q side chains interacting specifically with other Q side chains.
claims.source: We next asked if the odd-even effect concerns the Q side chains themselves, rather than their interaction with Ns, by replacing the Ns with residues of diverse physicochemistry—either glycine, alanine, serine, or histidine. Again, nucleation was much more frequent for Q3X and Q5X than for Q4X (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), confirming that the odd-even effect resulted from the Q side chains interacting specifically with other Q side chains.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments with different amino acid substitutions.

claims.claim: The nucleus is encoded by segments of sequence with Qs at every other position.
claims.source: The relative indifference of Q3X and Q5X to the identity of X suggests that these sequences form a pure Q core that excludes every other side chain. In other words, the nucleus is encoded by segments of sequence with Qs at every other position.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data on Q3X and Q5X sequences.

claims.claim: Amyloid formation broadly increased in [PIN+] cells compared to [pin-] cells.
claims.source: To reduce the contribution of the conformational fluctuation to nucleation, we next performed DAmFRET experiments for all sequences in [PIN+] cells. Amyloid formation broadly increased (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B)
claims.evidence: This is an observation from DAmFRET experiments in [PIN+] cells.

claims.claim: PolyQ now nucleates in most [PIN+] cells even at the lowest concentrations sampled by DAmFRET (~1 µM).
claims.source: with polyQ now nucleating in most [PIN+] cells even at the lowest concentrations sampled by DAmFRET (~1 µM, Khan et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from DAmFRET experiments in [PIN+] cells.

claims.claim: Amyloid formation in [PIN+] retained the structural constraints of de novo nucleation.
claims.source: Additionally, nucleation in [PIN+] retained the structural constraints of de novo nucleation, as indicated by (a) the relative impacts of different X substitutions, which again increased in the order serine <alanine < histidine <glycine/asparagine; and (b) the persistence of the odd-even effect, with q=1, 3, and 5 nucleating more frequently than q=4.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from comparing DAmFRET experiments in [PIN+] and [pin-] cells.

claims.claim: Most amyloid predictors failed to detect amyloid propensity in polyQ sequences.
claims.source: In fact, most predictors failed outright to detect amyloid propensity in this class of sequences.
claims.evidence: This is a result from testing various amyloid prediction algorithms on polyQ sequences.

claims.claim: None of the amyloid predictors were able to distinguish Q3N and Q5N from Q4N.
claims.source: Unfortunately, none of the predictors were able to distinguish Q3N and Q5N from Q4N (Supplementary file 2), despite their very dissimilar experimentally determined amyloid propensities.
claims.evidence: This is a result from testing various amyloid prediction algorithms.

claims.claim: Structural investigations of predominantly Q-containing amyloid cores reveal an exquisitely ordered tertiary motif wherein columns of Q side chains from each sheet fully extend and interdigitate with those of the opposing sheet.
claims.source: Structural investigations of predominantly Q-containing amyloid cores reveal an exquisitely ordered tertiary motif wherein columns of Q side chains from each sheet fully extend and interdigitate with those of the opposing sheet (Hoop et al., 2016; Schneider et al., 2011; Sikorski and Atkins, 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to structural studies.

claims.claim: The terminal amides of Q side chains form regular hydrogen bonds to the backbones of the opposing β-sheet.
claims.source: Additionally, the terminal amides of Q side chains form regular hydrogen bonds to the backbones of the opposing β-sheet (Esposito et al., 2008; Hervas et al., 2020; Man et al., 2015; Schneider et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2016b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to structural studies.

claims.claim: The Q zipper was highly specific for Q side chains and rapidly dissolved when any proximal pair of inward pointing Qs were substituted.
claims.source: In agreement with the experimental data, the Q zipper was highly specific for Q side chains: it rapidly dissolved when any proximal pair of inward pointing Qs were substituted, as would occur for unilaterally discontinuous sequences such as Q4X (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a result from molecular dynamics simulations.

claims.claim: The Q zipper remained intact when any number of outward-pointing Q residues were substituted.
claims.source: In contrast, it remained intact when any number of outward-pointing Q residues were substituted, as would occur for Q3X and Q5X.
claims.evidence: This is a result from molecular dynamics simulations.

claims.claim: The S-containing zipper remained intact while the N-containing zipper dissolved.
claims.source: In this case, the S-containing zipper remained intact while the N-containing zipper dissolved (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), consistent with our experimental results.
claims.evidence: This is a result from molecular dynamics simulations of four-stranded zippers.

claims.claim: When inside a Q zipper, the N side chain is too short to H-bond the opposing backbone.
claims.source: When inside a Q zipper, the N side chain is too short to H-bond the opposing backbone.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from molecular dynamics simulations.

claims.claim: The terminal amide of N competed against the adjacent backbone amides for H-bonding with the terminal amide of an opposing Q side-chain, blocking that side chain from fully extending as required for Q zipper stability.
claims.source: In our simulations, the terminal amide of N competed against the adjacent backbone amides for H-bonding with the terminal amide of an opposing Q side-chain, blocking that side chain from fully extending as required for Q zipper stability (Figure 2E–F).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from molecular dynamics simulations.

claims.claim: The side chain of S does not intercept H-bonds from the side chains of opposing Q residues.
claims.source: We found that the side chain of S, which is slightly shorter and less bulky than that of N, does not intercept H-bonds from the side chains of opposing Q residues (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from molecular dynamics simulations.

claims.claim: There is no evidence that Q side chains preferentially H-bond adjacent N side chains.
claims.source: This analysis showed no evidence that Q side chains preferentially H-bond adjacent N side chains (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D–E), ruling out the polar clasp mechanism of inhibition.
claims.evidence: This is a result from analysis of molecular dynamics simulations.

claims.claim: Molecular simulations are consistent with polyQ amyloid nucleating from a single Q zipper comprising two β-sheets engaged across an interface of fully interdigitated Q side chains.
claims.source: In sum, our simulations are consistent with polyQ amyloid nucleating from a single Q zipper comprising two β-sheets engaged across an interface of fully interdigitated Q side chains.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the molecular dynamics simulations.

claims.claim: PolyQ amyloids have a lamellar or 'slab-like' architecture.
claims.source: Prior structural studies show that polyQ amyloids have a lamellar or 'slab-like' architecture (Boatz et al., 2020; Galaz-Montoya et al., 2021; Nazarov et al., 2022; Sathasivam et al., 2010; Sharma et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claims.claim: Sequences with q values larger than 5 generally reached higher AmFRET values than those with q=3 or 5.
claims.source: We observed that when expressed to high concentrations, sequences with q values larger than 5 generally reached higher AmFRET values than those with q=3 or 5 (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from DAmFRET experiments.

claims.claim: PolyQ and Q7N achieved higher AmFRET than Q3N regardless of linker terminus and identity.
claims.source: To control for the latter, we varied the terminus and type of linker used to attach mEos3.1 to polyQ, Q3N, and Q7N. We found that polyQ and Q7N achieved higher AmFRET than Q3N regardless of linker terminus and identity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments with different linker configurations.

claims.claim: The high AmFRET level achieved by polyQ amyloids results from the subunits occurring in closer proximity than in amyloids that lack the ability to form lamella.
claims.source: The high AmFRET level achieved by polyQ amyloids therefore results from the subunits occurring in closer proximity than in amyloids that lack the ability to form lamella.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the AmFRET data with different linker configurations.

claims.claim: QU amyloid particles were smaller than those of QB.
claims.source: We found that QU amyloid particles were smaller than those of QB (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from SDD-AGE experiments.

claims.claim: Cells with intermediate AmFRET values were less frequent for QU.
claims.source: To compare growth rates, we examined AmFRET histograms through the bimodal region of DAmFRET plots for [pin-] cells. Cells with intermediate AmFRET values (i.e. cells in which amyloid had nucleated but not yet reached steady state) were less frequent for QU (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C)
claims.evidence: This is an observation from DAmFRET experiments.

claims.claim: The SDD-AGE data are most consistent with increased fragmentation of QU amyloids.
claims.source: Therefore, the SDD-AGE data are most consistent with the third possibility—increased fragmentation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the SDD-AGE and DAmFRET data.

claims.claim: QB amyloids have a lamellar architecture with more than two β-sheets.
claims.source: Based on the fact that larger amyloid cores, such as those with multiple steric zippers, oppose fragmentation (Tanaka et al., 2006; Verges et al., 2011; Zanjani et al., 2020), these data therefore suggest that QB amyloids have a lamellar (Figure 3A) architecture with more than two β-sheets.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the fragmentation data and prior knowledge about amyloid cores.

claims.claim: The frequency of amyloid formation plateaued at intermediate concentrations before increasing again at higher concentrations.
claims.source: While all sequences formed amyloid more frequently with concentration in the low regime, as concentrations increased further, the frequency of amyloid formation plateaued somewhat before increasing again at higher concentrations (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from DAmFRET experiments.

claims.claim: A multiphasic dependence of amyloid formation on concentration implies that some higher-order species inhibits nucleation and/or growth.
claims.source: A multiphasic dependence of amyloid formation on concentration implies that some higher-order species inhibits nucleation and/or growth (Vitalis and Pappu, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Vitalis and Pappu, 2011.

claims.claim: Cells lacking AmFRET contained exclusively diffuse protein (no detectable puncta), even at high expression.
claims.source: To our surprise, however, cells lacking AmFRET contained exclusively diffuse protein (no detectable puncta), even at high expression (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from microscopy experiments.

claims.claim: Naive polyQ does not itself phase separate under normal cellular conditions.
claims.source: This means that naive polyQ does not itself phase separate under normal cellular conditions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the microscopy data showing no puncta in cells lacking AmFRET.

claims.claim: Q zipper nuclei appear to form dead-end (kinetically trapped) oligomers when the concentration of soluble polyQ is too high.
claims.source: That these oligomers are too sparse to detect by AmFRET, even at high total protein concentration, further suggests that their formation is kinetically limited, and, therefore, subsequent to Q zipper formation. In other words, Q zipper nuclei appear to form dead-end (kinetically trapped) oligomers when the concentration of soluble polyQ is too high.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the DAmFRET and microscopy data.

claims.claim: Q5N but not Q7N formed amyloid robustly at low concentrations.
claims.source: Specifically, we noticed that Q5N but not Q7N formed amyloid robustly at low concentrations (Figure 4A, purple arrow).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from DAmFRET experiments.

claims.claim: The anomalous solubility of Q7N coincides with the expected enhancement of self-poisoning at the transition between single long Q zippers and short lamellar Q zippers.
claims.source: We then realized, however, that the anomalous solubility of Q7N coincides with the expected enhancement of self-poisoning at the transition between single long Q zippers (favored by QU sequences) and short lamellar Q zippers (favored by QB sequences).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the DAmFRET data and knowledge of polymer crystallization.

claims.claim: QB sequences increasingly escaped the poisoned state as the potential length of lamellar strands increased beyond the minimum.
claims.source: Consistent with the behaviors of other self-poisoning polymers, QB sequences increasingly escaped the poisoned state as the potential length of lamellar strands increased beyond the minimum, i.e. with increasing q values beyond 6 (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from DAmFRET experiments.

claims.claim: Only sequences with at least five unilaterally contiguous Qs, or at least six bilaterally contiguous Qs, nucleated in [pin-] cells.
claims.source: We found that, while all sequences formed amyloid with a detectable frequency in [PIN+] cells, only those with at least five unilaterally contiguous Qs, or at least six bilaterally contiguous Qs, did so in [pin-] cells.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from DAmFRET experiments with sequences of restricted contiguity.

claims.claim: The threshold strand length is nine or ten residues for single Q zippers to propagate, and six residues for lamellar Q zippers to propagate.
claims.source: Given that the ability to nucleate in the absence of a pre-existing conformational template is characteristic of Q zippers, this result is consistent with a threshold strand length of nine or ten residues for single Q zippers to propagate, and six residues for lamellar Q zippers to propagate.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the contiguity experiments.

claims.claim: Treated AmFRET-positive cells in the bifurcated regime achieved higher AmFRET values than cells whose translation was not arrested.
claims.source: As predicted, treated AmFRET-positive cells in the bifurcated regime achieved higher AmFRET values than cells whose translation was not arrested (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from experiments with translation inhibitors.

claims.claim: A minimal intramolecular Q zipper would comprise a pair of two-stranded β-sheets connected by loops of approximately four residues.
claims.source: A minimal intramolecular Q zipper would comprise a pair of two-stranded β-sheets connected by loops of approximately four residues (Chou and Fasman, 1977; Hennetin et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural knowledge and citations.

claims.claim: If the clinical threshold of approximately 36 residues is the length required to form an intramolecular Q zipper, then the strands must be approximately six residues with three unilaterally contiguous Qs.
claims.source: If we take the clinical threshold of approximately 36 residues as the length required to form this structure, then the strands must be approximately six residues with three unilaterally contiguous Qs—exactly the length we deduced for intramolecular strand formation in the previous section.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the clinical threshold and the experimental findings.

claims.claim: The Q4N appendage increased the fraction of cells in the high-AmFRET population relative to those expressing Q3N alone.
claims.source: As predicted, the Q4N appendage increased the fraction of cells in the high-AmFRET population relative to those expressing Q3N alone, and even more so relative to those expressing the Q2N-appended protein (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from DAmFRET experiments with Q4N appendages.

claims.claim: The experimental data are consistent with a single short Q zipper as the amyloid nucleus.
claims.source: These data are consistent with a single short Q zipper as the amyloid nucleus.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the Q4N appendage experiments.

claims.claim: The oDi fusion reduced amyloid formation, and the FTH1 fusion all but eliminated it, for both QU and QB sequences.
claims.source: Remarkably, the oDi fusion reduced amyloid formation, and the FTH1 fusion all but eliminated it, for both QU and QB sequences (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from DAmFRET experiments with oligomeric fusions.

claims.claim: The inhibitory effect of oDi manifested regardless of the terminus tagged or the linker used.
claims.source: The inhibitory effect of oDi manifested regardless of the terminus tagged or the linker used, and the inhibitory effect was suppressed by the monomerizing mutation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–F)
claims.evidence: This is an observation from control experiments with different linkers and termini.

claims.claim: Preemptive oligomerization inhibits amyloid nucleation.
claims.source: altogether confirming that preemptive oligomerization inhibits amyloid nucleation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the oligomeric fusion experiments.

claims.claim: The minimal polyQ amyloid nucleus sequence formed amyloid robustly, with a concentration-dependence and [PIN+]-independence characteristic of QB.
claims.source: We found that the protein indeed formed amyloid robustly, and with a concentration-dependence and [PIN+]-independence that is characteristic of QB (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from DAmFRET experiments with the synthetic minimal nucleus.

claims.claim: Mutating a single Q residue to an N in the minimal nucleus completely eliminated amyloid formation.
claims.source: We therefore mutated a single Q residue to an N. Remarkably, this tiny change—removing just one carbon atom from the polypeptide—completely eliminated amyloid formation (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from DAmFRET experiments with the mutated minimal nucleus.

claims.claim: The polyQ amyloid nucleus is an intramolecular Q zipper.
claims.source: We conclude that the polyQ amyloid nucleus is an intramolecular Q zipper.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all the experimental data.

claims.claim: Amyloid formation by pathologically expanded polyQ begins with the formation of a minimal steric zipper of interdigitated side chains within a single polypeptide molecule.
claims.source: Collectively our data demonstrate that amyloid formation by pathologically expanded polyQ begins with the formation of a minimal steric zipper of interdigitated side chains—a 'Q zipper'—within a single polypeptide molecule.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, summarizing all the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Amyloid formation by polyQ resembles the crystallization of long synthetic homopolymers in dilute solution.
claims.source: In this respect, amyloid formation by polyQ resembles the crystallization of long synthetic homopolymers in dilute solution (Hu, 2018; Hu et al., 2003; Lauritzen and Hoffman, 1960).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison supported by citations to polymer crystallization literature.

claims.claim: Kinetic studies performed in vitro and in neuronal cell culture have found that polyQ aggregates with a reaction order of approximately one.
claims.source: Kinetic studies performed in vitro (Bhattacharyya et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2002; Kar et al., 2011) and in neuronal cell culture Colby et al., 2006 have found that polyQ aggregates with a reaction order of approximately one.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior kinetic studies.

claims.claim: A recent study investigating the aggregation kinetics of Q40-YFP in C. elegans body wall muscle cells observed a reaction order of 1.6.
claims.source: A recent study investigating the aggregation kinetics of Q40-YFP in C. elegans body wall muscle cells observed a reaction order of 1.6 (Sinnige et al., 2021)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sinnige et al., 2021.

claims.claim: The rate-limiting step for pathologic polyQ amyloid formation occurs within a monomer.
claims.source: By explicitly manipulating concentration, length, density and conformational heterogeneities, we confirm that the rate-limiting step for pathologic polyQ amyloid formation does indeed occur within a monomer.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental manipulations described in the study.

claims.claim: The rate-limiting step for pathologic polyQ amyloid formation occurs within a monomer even in the dynamic, intermingled, living cellular environment.
claims.source: Moreover, we show that it does so even in the dynamic, intermingled, living cellular environment.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion emphasizing that the findings apply in living cells.

claims.claim: The short-stranded nucleus is a catalyst for longer, lamellar Q zippers that make up the amyloid core.
claims.source: In the case of polyQ, the short-stranded nucleus is a catalyst for longer, lamellar Q zippers that make up the amyloid core.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data on strand length requirements.

claims.claim: The minimally competent zipper provides lower bounds on the widths of fibers—they can be as thin as two sheets (1.6 nm) and as short as six residues.
claims.source: The minimally competent zipper identified here provides lower bounds on the widths of fibers—they can be as thin as two sheets (1.6 nm) and as short as six residues.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the minimal nucleus structure.

claims.claim: Pathologic polyQ or huntingtin amyloids feature a slab-like architecture with restrictions as thin as 2 nm and as short as five residues.
claims.source: Remarkably, observations from recent cryoEM tomography studies closely match this prediction: pathologic polyQ or huntingtin amyloids, whether in cells or in vitro, feature a slab-like architecture with restrictions as thin as 2  nm (Galaz-Montoya et al., 2021) and as short as five residues (Nazarov et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent structural studies.

claims.claim: Multidimensional polymer crystal growth offers a simple explanation for the characteristically antiparallel arrangement of strands in polyQ amyloid.
claims.source: Multidimensional polymer crystal growth offers a simple explanation for the characteristically antiparallel arrangement of strands in polyQ amyloid.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on polymer crystallization principles.

claims.claim: If lamella are responsible for antiparallel strands, then QU sequences should form typical amyloid fibers with parallel β-strands.
claims.source: If lamella are responsible for antiparallel strands, then QU sequences should form typical amyloid fibers with parallel β-strands.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the lamellar growth model.

claims.claim: The only atomic resolution structure of a Q zipper amyloid is of a protein with striking unilateral (but not bilateral) contiguity, and the strands are parallel.
claims.source: The only atomic resolution structure of a Q zipper amyloid happens to be of a protein with striking unilateral (but not bilateral) contiguity (Hervas et al., 2020), and the strands are parallel as predicted.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hervas et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The flanking regions and other features of full-length proteins have been shown to modulate both the aggregation and toxicity of polyQ.
claims.source: The flanking regions and other features of full-length proteins have been shown to modulate both the aggregation and toxicity of polyQ (Adegbuyiro et al., 2017; Arndt et al., 2020; Ceccon et al., 2022; Elena-Real et al., 2023a; Elena-Real et al., 2023b; Hong et al., 2019; Khaled et al., 2023; Kuiper et al., 2017; Lieberman et al., 2019; Silva et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The intrinsic behavior of the polyQ tract itself is central to pathology.
claims.source: Nevertheless, that the intrinsic behavior of the polyQ tract itself is central to pathology is evident from the fact that the nine pathologic polyQ proteins have similar length thresholds despite different functions, flanking domains, interaction partners, and expression levels.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the observation that different polyQ proteins have similar length thresholds.

claims.claim: Only two of the nine polyQ diseases have length thresholds below the minimum length for an intramolecular Q zipper.
claims.source: Only two of the nine polyQ diseases have length thresholds below the minimum length for an intramolecular Q zipper as deduced here (Lieberman et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of the deduced minimum length with known disease thresholds, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: SCA2 and SCA6 disease onset is accelerated in homozygous individuals.
claims.source: These two proteins—SCA2 (32 residues) and SCA6 (21 residues)—also appear to be atypical for this class of diseases in that disease onset is accelerated in homozygous individuals (Laffita-Mesa et al., 2012; Mariotti et al., 2001; Soga et al., 2017; Spadafora et al., 2007; Tojima et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The accelerated disease onset in homozygous individuals for SCA2 and SCA6 is consistent with nucleation occurring in oligomers.
claims.source: This is consistent with nucleation occurring in oligomers, as would be necessary for polyQ tracts that are too short to form all four strands of the minimal Q zipper within one molecule.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the observation of accelerated disease onset in homozygous individuals.

claims.claim: Among the hundreds of amyloid-forming proteins characterized by DAmFRET, only Cyc8 PrD has a similar concentration-dependence to polyQ.
claims.source: Among the hundreds of amyloid-forming proteins we have now characterized by DAmFRET (Khan et al., 2018; Posey et al., 2021, and unpublished), only Cyc8 PrD has a similar concentration-dependence.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison based on unpublished data from the authors' lab.

claims.claim: The similar concentration-dependence of Cyc8 PrD is attributed to self-poisoning due to its exceptionally long tract of 50 unilaterally contiguous Qs.
claims.source: We now attribute this to self-poisoning due to its exceptionally long tract of 50 unilaterally contiguous Qs, primarily in the form of QA dipeptide repeats.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the sequence of Cyc8 PrD and the findings on self-poisoning.

claims.claim: Soluble oligomers accumulate during the aggregation of pathologically lengthened polyQ and/or Htt in vitro, in cultured cells, and in the brains of patients.
claims.source: Soluble oligomers accumulate during the aggregation of pathologically lengthened polyQ and/or Htt in vitro, in cultured cells, and in the brains of patients (Auer et al., 2008; Hsieh et al., 2017; Legleiter et al., 2010; Levin et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2018; Li et al., 2010; Olshina et al., 2010; Sathasivam et al., 2010; Sil et al., 2018; Takahashi et al., 2008; Vitalis and Pappu, 2011; Yamaguchi et al., 2005; Zanjani et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Soluble oligomers are likely culprits of proteotoxicity.
claims.source: They are likely culprits of proteotoxicity (Kim et al., 2016; Leitman et al., 2013; Lu and Palacino, 2013; Matlahov and Matlahov and van der Wel, 2019; Takahashi et al., 2008; Wetzel, 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: All forms of multimerization appeared to be dependent on Q zipper nucleation.
claims.source: We did not observe disordered oligomerization in cells. Instead, all forms of multimerization appeared to be dependent on Q zipper nucleation.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Kinetically arrested aggregates emerge from the same event that limits the rate of amyloid formation.
claims.source: That kinetically arrested aggregates emerge from the same event that limits the rate of amyloid formation suggests a resolution to the paradox that polyQ diseases are characterized by amyloid formation despite the implication of non-amyloid species (Kim et al., 2016; Leitman et al., 2013; Lu and Palacino, 2013; Matlahov and Matlahov and van der Wel, 2019; Takahashi et al., 2008; Wetzel, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the experimental findings on self-poisoning.

claims.claim: The decades-long course of clinical disease provides an upper limit on the timescale of candidate proteopathic events.
claims.source: The decades-long course of clinical disease provides an upper limit on the timescale of candidate proteopathic events.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the timescale of disease based on clinical knowledge.

claims.claim: The event of Q zipper nucleation could in principle dominate the kinetics of disease even if it occurs as rarely as once per neuron over the lifetime of a patient.
claims.source: Because of this long timescale, the event of Q zipper nucleation—even if it occurs as rarely as once per neuron over the lifetime of a patient—could in principle dominate the kinetics of disease.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the long timescale of disease.

claims.claim: A slow-growing self-poisoned Q zipper may very well take years to kill the neuron.
claims.source: Likewise, a slow-growing self-poisoned Q zipper may very well take years to kill the neuron.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the self-poisoning mechanism.

claims.claim: Overexpression plausibly changes the nature of the toxic species and triggers pathways of cell death that may be irrelevant to disease.
claims.source: By circumventing the self-poisoned state, overexpression plausibly changes the nature of the toxic species and triggers pathways of cell death that may be irrelevant to disease.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the effects of overexpression in disease models.

claims.claim: The ideal model for polyQ diseases will accelerate Q zipper nucleation without changing amyloid equilibrium.
claims.source: From our perspective, the ideal model for polyQ diseases will accelerate Q zipper nucleation without changing amyloid equilibrium, as could be achieved by expressing a synthetic Q zipper template.
claims.evidence: This is a suggestion for future disease models based on the findings.

claims.claim: PolyQ (absent flanking domains) does not phase separate prior to amyloid formation in cells.
claims.source: our findings corroborate prior demonstrations that polyQ (absent flanking domains) does not phase separate prior to amyloid formation in cells, whether expressed in human neuronal cells (Colby et al., 2006; Kakkar et al., 2016), C. elegans body wall muscle cells (Sinnige et al., 2021), or [pin-] yeast cells (Duennwald et al., 2006a; Jiang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: Full-length Huntingtin protein with a pathologically lengthened polyQ tract does phase separate in cells.
claims.source: In contrast, full-length Huntingtin protein with a pathologically lengthened polyQ tract does phase separate in cells (Aktar et al., 2019; de Mattos et al., 2022; Peskett et al., 2018; Wan et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: If mutant Huntingtin forms an endogenous condensate when expressed from just one allele, then the buffering effect of phase separation will prevent a second allele from increasing the concentration of nucleation-competent monomers.
claims.source: Specifically, if mutant Huntingtin forms an endogenous condensate (if only in some microcompartment of the cell) when expressed from just one allele, then the buffering effect of phase separation (Klosin et al., 2020) will prevent a second allele from increasing the concentration of nucleation-competent monomers.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the lack of gene dosage effect in Huntington's Disease.

claims.claim: The multimers are nascent amyloids that templated their own arrest in the earliest stages of growth following nucleation.
claims.source: In short, the multimers are nascent amyloids that templated their own arrest in the earliest stages of growth following nucleation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the self-poisoning mechanism.

claims.claim: Pappu and colleagues found that polyQ populates a soluble phase of large spherical oligomers at concentrations that are slightly subsaturated with respect to fibrils.
claims.source: Our observations that arrested post-nucleated species commence growth at higher concentrations echoes in vitro findings by Pappu and colleagues that polyQ populates a soluble phase of large spherical oligomers at concentrations that are slightly subsaturated with respect to fibrils (Crick et al., 2013; Posey et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Crick et al., 2013 and Posey et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The authors offer an alternative interpretation of large oligomers as the partially ordered products of self-poisoned nucleation.
claims.source: We therefore offer an alternative interpretation of these large oligomers, namely, as the partially ordered products of self-poisoned nucleation.
claims.evidence: This is a new interpretation proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claims.claim: The existence of a lower phase boundary for large oligomers is consistent with findings that intra- and intermolecular Q zippers have different critical lengths.
claims.source: The existence of a lower phase boundary for these species is consistent with our findings that intra- and intermolecular Q zippers have different critical lengths, which follows from the fact that intramolecular segments are covalently constrained to much higher effective concentrations that allow for intramolecular β-sheets to have shorter strands.
claims.evidence: This is an inference connecting the phase boundary to the critical length findings.

claims.claim: A recent study using cryogenic nanoprobe small angle X-ray scattering revealed a population of soluble oligomers with features of stacked β-sheets.
claims.source: Consistent with this expectation, a recent study using cryogenic nanoprobe small angle X-ray scattering to probe the structure of unlabeled mutant Htt exon 1 in cells revealed a population of soluble oligomers with features of stacked β-sheets (Rumancev et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rumancev et al., 2021.

claims.claim: The role of contralateral zippers in the formation of aborted amyloids is consistent with the apparent protective effect of CAT trinucleotide insertions in SCA1.
claims.source: However, the role of contralateral zippers in their formation is consistent with the apparent protective effect of CAT trinucleotide insertions that preserve unilateral contiguity (QHQHQH) in the polyQ disease protein, SCA1 (Menon et al., 2013; Nethisinghe et al., 2018; Sen et al., 2003)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on SCA1.

claims.claim: The only known functional Q zipper—that of the neuronal translational regulator, Orb2—lacks bilateral contiguity.
claims.source: and the absence of bilateral contiguity in the only known functional Q zipper—that of the neuronal translational regulator, Orb2 (Hervas et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hervas et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The toxicity of polyQ amyloid arises from its lamellar architecture.
claims.source: We speculate that the toxicity of polyQ amyloid arises from its lamellar architecture.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation by the authors based on their findings.

claims.claim: Current therapeutic efforts focused on lowering the levels of mutant Huntingtin have not been successful.
claims.source: Current therapeutic efforts focused on lowering the levels of mutant Huntingtin have not been successful.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current state of therapeutic efforts based on knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Therapies designed to oligomerize huntingtin preemptively will delay nucleation and thereby decelerate the disease.
claims.source: As an admittedly radical alternative, we suggest that therapies designed to (further) oligomerize huntingtin preemptively will delay nucleation and thereby decelerate the disease.
claims.evidence: This is a therapeutic suggestion based on the findings about oligomerization inhibiting nucleation.

results.result: PolyQ is an amyloid-forming sequence responsible for nine fatal neurodegenerative diseases in humans, including Huntington's Disease, and amyloid self-templating drives disease progression.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 establish the background on polyQ diseases through established knowledge (C1, C4) and well-supported citations (C2, C3). These are foundational claims that set the context for the study.

results.result: PolyQ pathology exhibits stochastic cell death with constant frequency, aggregation occurs stochastically, disease is determined by glutamine expansion beyond ~36 residues, and severity does not worsen with gene dosage, implying the rate-determining step occurs in a minor fraction of molecules.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C9 are well-supported by multiple citations to prior work. The inference in C9 logically follows from the gene dosage observation in C8. These establish key features of polyQ disease that motivate the study.

results.result: Amyloid nuclei cannot be directly observed, are unstable by definition, their structures do not necessarily correspond to mature amyloids, and nucleation cannot be simulated with high resolution from a naive state.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C13 establish the technical challenges in studying amyloid nucleation through established knowledge (C10, C11) and citations (C12, C13). These justify the need for the experimental approach used in this study.

results.result: Amyloid formation involves loss of intramolecular entropy, nucleation selects specific conformations, proteins can accumulate to supersaturating concentrations while remaining soluble, nucleation tends to occur heterogeneously via metastable intermediates, and current opinion holds that heterogeneities involve liquid-liquid phase separation.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C20 establish the theoretical framework for understanding amyloid nucleation through established knowledge and extensive citations. These provide the conceptual foundation for interpreting the experimental results.

results.result: DAmFRET experiments show that Q60 cells partition into populations with or without amyloid in a bimodal distribution that persists at the same protein concentration, indicating nucleation-limited amyloid formation. Q lengths ≤35 lack AmFRET while Q≥40 acquire AmFRET in a length and concentration-dependent manner, recapitulating the pathologic threshold. N60 shows much lower nucleation frequency than Q60.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C23, C28-C30 present core experimental observations from DAmFRET that validate the method and establish the pathologic threshold. The bimodal distribution and concentration-independence at fixed concentration strongly support nucleation-limited kinetics. The data are clearly shown in figures.

results.result: Nucleation of pathologically expanded polyQ involves segments of three glutamine residues at every other position. Amyloid formation for q<6 was limited to odd numbers (1, 3, 5), exhibiting an 'odd-even effect' that saturated at six. This odd-even effect results from Q side chains interacting specifically with other Q side chains, and the nucleus is encoded by segments with Qs at every other position.
results.evaluation: Claims C24, C31-C34 present the key discovery of the Q-at-every-other-position pattern through systematic Q/N sequence experiments. The odd-even effect is clearly demonstrated in the data (C31-C32), and experiments with different amino acid substitutions (C33) confirm Q-specific interactions. The inference to the pattern (C34) is well-supported.

results.result: Amyloid formation broadly increased in [PIN+] cells compared to [pin-] cells, with polyQ nucleating in most [PIN+] cells even at ~1 µM. Nucleation in [PIN+] retained the structural constraints of de novo nucleation, including the odd-even effect and relative impacts of different substitutions.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 demonstrate that the conformational template [PIN+] reduces the nucleation barrier but preserves the structural requirements identified in [pin-] cells. This validates that the pattern identified reflects the intrinsic nucleus structure. The data are shown in supplementary figures.

results.result: Most amyloid predictors failed to detect amyloid propensity in polyQ sequences, and none could distinguish Q3N and Q5N from Q4N despite their very different experimental amyloid propensities.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 demonstrate that existing computational methods fail for polyQ, supporting the need for the experimental approach. The data are provided in Supplementary file 2. This highlights the unique nature of polyQ nucleation.

results.result: Molecular dynamics simulations demonstrate that the Q zipper structure involves interdigitated Q side chains with regular hydrogen bonds to opposing backbones. The zipper is highly specific for Q side chains, dissolving when inward-pointing Qs are substituted but remaining intact when outward-pointing Qs are substituted. N disrupts the zipper because its side chain is too short to H-bond the opposing backbone but intercepts H-bonds from opposing Q side chains. S does not disrupt the zipper because it does not intercept these H-bonds.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C49 present molecular dynamics simulations that explain the structural basis for the odd-even effect and the differential effects of N vs S substitutions. The simulations are well-described in methods and results are shown in figures. The mechanism by which N disrupts the zipper (C45-C46) is clearly demonstrated, and the polar clasp mechanism is ruled out (C48). The conclusion (C49) is well-supported by the simulation data.

results.result: PolyQ amyloids have a lamellar architecture. Sequences with q>5 (QB) reached higher AmFRET values than q=3 or 5 (QU), regardless of linker configuration, indicating higher subunit density consistent with lamellar structure. QU amyloid particles were smaller than QB by SDD-AGE, with fewer cells at intermediate AmFRET values, consistent with increased fragmentation. This suggests QB amyloids have a lamellar architecture with more than two β-sheets.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C57 establish that QB sequences form lamellar structures while QU sequences form single zippers. The AmFRET data (C51-C53) with linker controls are convincing. The SDD-AGE data (C54) and growth rate analysis (C55) support the fragmentation interpretation (C56). The inference to lamellar architecture (C57) is well-reasoned based on prior knowledge about fragmentation resistance.

results.result: The frequency of amyloid formation plateaued at intermediate concentrations before increasing again at higher concentrations, implying that some higher-order species inhibits nucleation/growth. Cells lacking AmFRET contained exclusively diffuse protein with no detectable puncta even at high expression, indicating that naive polyQ does not phase separate under normal cellular conditions. Q zipper nuclei appear to form dead-end oligomers when soluble polyQ concentration is too high.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C62 present the discovery of self-poisoning in polyQ aggregation. The multiphasic concentration dependence (C58) is clearly shown in Figure 4A. The microscopy data (C60) definitively rule out phase separation, contradicting a major hypothesis in the field. The inference to kinetically trapped oligomers (C62) is well-reasoned from the data.

results.result: Q5N but not Q7N formed amyloid robustly at low concentrations. The anomalous solubility of Q7N coincides with expected enhancement of self-poisoning at the transition between single long Q zippers and short lamellar Q zippers. QB sequences increasingly escaped the poisoned state as the potential length of lamellar strands increased beyond the minimum (q>6).
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65 explain the self-poisoning phenomenon through analogy to polymer crystallization. The observation (C63) is clear in Figure 4A. The interpretation (C64) connecting this to the transition between zipper types is creative and well-reasoned. The escape from poisoning (C65) is demonstrated in Figure 4D.

results.result: Only sequences with at least five unilaterally contiguous Qs, or at least six bilaterally contiguous Qs, nucleated in [pin-] cells. This is consistent with a threshold strand length of nine or ten residues for single Q zippers to propagate, and six residues for lamellar Q zippers to propagate.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 establish critical strand lengths through systematic contiguity experiments. The data are shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D. The inference to different critical lengths for intra- vs intermolecular zippers (C67) is well-reasoned.

results.result: Translation inhibition caused AmFRET-positive cells in the bifurcated regime to achieve higher AmFRET values than untreated cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C68 provides experimental support for the self-poisoning model by showing that stopping new protein synthesis allows poisoned aggregates to mature. The data are shown in Figure 4E and supplement.

results.result: A minimal intramolecular Q zipper would comprise a pair of two-stranded β-sheets connected by loops of approximately four residues. If the clinical threshold of ~36 residues is the length required to form an intramolecular Q zipper, then the strands must be approximately six residues with three unilaterally contiguous Qs—exactly the length deduced for intramolecular strand formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 connect the experimental findings to the clinical threshold through structural reasoning. The calculation is straightforward and the match between predicted and observed strand lengths is striking, providing strong support for the intramolecular nucleus model.

results.result: Appending Q4N to Q3N increased the fraction of cells in the high-AmFRET population relative to Q3N alone or Q2N-appended protein. This is consistent with a single short Q zipper as the amyloid nucleus.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 provide a clever test of whether the nucleus is a single short zipper. The data in Figure 5A show the predicted effect. This supports the model that Q4N can contribute strands to a nucleus but cannot propagate on its own.

results.result: Genetic fusion to oligomeric proteins (oDi dimer or FTH1 24-mer) reduced or eliminated amyloid formation for both QU and QB sequences. The inhibitory effect manifested regardless of terminus or linker and was suppressed by a monomerizing mutation, confirming that preemptive oligomerization inhibits amyloid nucleation.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 demonstrate that oligomerization prior to nucleation blocks amyloid formation. The data in Figure 5B and supplements include appropriate controls (different termini, linkers, monomerizing mutation). This strongly supports an intramolecular nucleus.

results.result: A synthetic minimal polyQ amyloid nucleus sequence (four tracts of six Qs linked by three glycines) formed amyloid robustly with QB-like behavior. Mutating a single Q to N completely eliminated amyloid formation. This demonstrates that the polyQ amyloid nucleus is an intramolecular Q zipper, and amyloid formation begins with formation of a minimal steric zipper within a single polypeptide molecule.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 present the culminating experiment that validates the entire model. The synthetic minimal nucleus forms amyloid as predicted (C76), and a single Q-to-N mutation abolishes activity (C77), demonstrating exquisite specificity. The conclusions (C78-C79) are strongly supported by all the experimental data.

results.result: Amyloid formation by polyQ resembles crystallization of long synthetic homopolymers. Prior kinetic studies found reaction order ~1, and by manipulating concentration, length, density and conformational heterogeneities, this study confirms that the rate-limiting step occurs within a monomer, even in the living cellular environment.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C84 connect the findings to prior kinetic studies and polymer physics. The citations to prior work (C81-C82) support reaction order ~1. The conclusion (C83-C84) is well-supported by the totality of experimental manipulations in the study.

results.result: The short-stranded nucleus catalyzes longer, lamellar Q zippers that make up the amyloid core. The minimal zipper provides lower bounds on fiber dimensions (as thin as two sheets/1.6 nm and as short as six residues). Recent cryoEM studies show pathologic polyQ amyloids have slab-like architecture with restrictions as thin as 2 nm and as short as five residues, matching these predictions.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 connect the nucleus structure to mature amyloid architecture. The inference (C85) is well-reasoned. The predicted dimensions (C86) match recent structural studies (C87), providing strong independent validation of the model.

results.result: Multidimensional polymer crystal growth explains the antiparallel strand arrangement in polyQ amyloid. If lamella are responsible for antiparallel strands, then QU sequences should form parallel β-strands. The only atomic resolution structure of a Q zipper amyloid is of a protein with unilateral contiguity, and the strands are parallel as predicted.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 make a testable prediction about strand orientation based on the lamellar growth model. The prediction (C89) is validated by existing structural data (C90), providing additional support for the model.

results.result: While flanking regions modulate polyQ aggregation and toxicity, the intrinsic behavior of the polyQ tract is central to pathology, as evidenced by similar length thresholds across nine diseases. Only two diseases (SCA2 and SCA6) have thresholds below the minimum for an intramolecular Q zipper, and these show accelerated disease onset in homozygous individuals, consistent with nucleation in oligomers.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C95 discuss the generalizability of the findings to disease. The argument (C92) is well-reasoned. The observation about SCA2 and SCA6 (C93-C94) and the interpretation (C95) provide additional support for the intramolecular nucleus model in most polyQ diseases.

results.result: Among hundreds of amyloid-forming proteins characterized by DAmFRET, only Cyc8 PrD has similar concentration-dependence to polyQ, attributed to self-poisoning due to its exceptionally long tract of 50 unilaterally contiguous Qs.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C97 compare polyQ to other amyloid-forming proteins. While C96 is based on the authors' extensive data, it includes unpublished results. The interpretation (C97) is reasonable but speculative without additional data on Cyc8 PrD.

results.result: Soluble oligomers accumulate during polyQ/Htt aggregation and are likely culprits of proteotoxicity. All forms of multimerization appeared dependent on Q zipper nucleation. Kinetically arrested aggregates emerge from the same event that limits amyloid formation, resolving the paradox that polyQ diseases are characterized by amyloid formation despite implication of non-amyloid species.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C101 connect the findings to disease mechanisms. Prior work on oligomers (C98-C99) is well-cited. The observation that multimerization depends on Q zipper nucleation (C100) is supported by the data. The synthesis (C101) provides a compelling resolution to a longstanding paradox.

results.result: The decades-long course of disease provides an upper limit on timescales of proteopathic events. Q zipper nucleation could dominate disease kinetics even if occurring once per neuron per lifetime. A slow-growing self-poisoned Q zipper may take years to kill neurons. Overexpression may change the toxic species and trigger irrelevant cell death pathways. The ideal disease model will accelerate Q zipper nucleation without changing amyloid equilibrium.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C106 discuss implications for disease timescales and models. C102 is factual. C103-C106 are speculations about disease mechanisms and model systems. While reasonable, these lack direct experimental support and represent future directions rather than established results.

results.result: PolyQ (absent flanking domains) does not phase separate prior to amyloid formation in cells, corroborating prior studies. In contrast, full-length Huntingtin with pathologically lengthened polyQ does phase separate. If mutant Huntingtin forms an endogenous condensate from one allele, phase separation buffering will prevent a second allele from increasing nucleation-competent monomer concentration.
